reason: The quotas row describes the maximum number of rules you can specify for an S3 lifecycle configuration as 1,000, not adjustable; claim, scope and display match.

The quotes support the 128 KB default, the per-object transition charge, the size filter and the pre-September-2024 behavior, but the context says configurations created before September 2024 keep the previous behavior unless modified; the claim says the new default applies since September 2024 and drops that condition.

The quotes define a Lifecycle configuration as a set of rules defining actions S3 applies to a group of objects and say rules can transition objects to less expensive storage classes, archive them or delete them.
Under Supported transitions the quote says that when access patterns are unknown or changing you can transition objects to S3 Intelligent-Tiering for automatic cost savings.
The quotes state the waterfall model and the enumerated supported transitions for S3 Standard, S3 One Zone-IA and S3 Glacier Flexible Retrieval exactly as the claim lists them.

The table row only marks Lifecycle transitions Yes/No per listed class without a direction; the claim reads it as transitions into every storage class, which the row does not say (S3 Standard is marked Yes yet is not a transition target in the waterfall list) and the table covers only eight classes.
The quote and its context state that accounts with an approved quota above 10,000 must send paginated ListBuckets requests and that unpaginated ones are rejected for them.
The quotes say Macie discovers sensitive data using machine learning and pattern matching and generates a security finding when it detects sensitive data in an S3 object.
The quote states verbatim that you cannot use MFA delete with lifecycle configurations.

The quote requires two forms of authentication from the bucket owner to delete a version or change the versioning state; the context lists permanently deleting an object version and changing the versioning state.
The quotes say only the bucket owner (root account) can enable MFA delete and that it cannot be enabled in the console; you must use the AWS CLI or the API.
The table row read against its header gives N/A, N/A, 1 hour, 30, 30, 90, 90 and 180 days for the eight classes in the order the claim states.

The FAQ quotes call Mountpoint an open source file client that mounts a bucket as a local file system, say it does not support modifying existing files or deleting existing directories, and that it is not suitable for multi-instance collaboration.
The limits table gives maximum number of parts per upload as 10,000.

The quotes support no expiry, explicit complete or stop, and independent, any-order, parallel parts, but the qualifier condition (unless a lifecycle rule aborts incomplete multipart uploads) appears in no quote or context.
The quote states verbatim that you can use a multipart upload for objects from 5 MB to 50 TB in size.
The limits table gives part numbers as 1 to 10,000 (inclusive).
The limits table gives part size 5 MiB to 5 GiB and says there is no minimum size limit on the last part.
The quote calls multipart upload a best practice for objects 100 MB or larger instead of a single operation; the second quote frames it as a recommendation.
The quotas row gives Multi-Region Access Points per account as 100 with Adjustable No.
The quotas row gives maximum Regions per Multi-Region Access Point as 20, not adjustable.

The pricing-page quote says MRAPs accelerate performance by up to 60% for data replicated across Regions and, based on Global Accelerator, route requests over the AWS network to the lowest latency copy.

The quote states a data routing cost per GB processed plus standard request, storage, data transfer and replication charges; the context names the separate internet acceleration cost in the condition.
The quote says the upload ID is required to upload parts, list parts, complete or stop an upload, and that anonymous users cannot initiate multipart uploads.
The quote supports paying for stored parts until you complete or stop the upload, but the qualifier condition (a lifecycle rule can abort incomplete multipart uploads) appears in no quote or context.
The quotes say you can upload parts in parallel to improve throughput and retransmit a failed part without affecting other parts.
The quotes state a set of parts uploaded independently and in any order, retransmission of a failed part, assembly after all parts, and the 100 MB best practice.

The quote supports objects with a unique identifier and metadata in an unstructured format, but the contrast 'not a hierarchy of blocks or a file tree' is not in the quote (blocks are not mentioned at all).
The quote supports the key as the unique identifier within the bucket, but does not say the key is set when you upload the object; that clause goes beyond the quote.
The quotes list the three alternatives verbatim and say all of them keep S3 as the underlying storage so no data migration is needed.

The quotes say a bucket retention period is a duration in days or years for every object version placed in the bucket, the Retain Until Date is creation time plus that duration, and explicit per-version settings override it.
The quotes state no user including root can overwrite or delete, the mode cannot change, the period cannot be shortened, and deleting the account is the only way to delete early.
The quotes give 403 Access Denied for a versioned DELETE, 200 OK plus a delete marker that becomes current for a simple DELETE on a protected object, and that delete markers are not WORM-protected.
The quotes say Object Lock can be enabled on an existing bucket via console, CLI, SDKs or REST API and that Object Lock works only with versioned buckets.

The quotes say users cannot overwrite, delete or alter lock settings without special permissions, and overriding requires s3:BypassGovernanceRetention plus the x-amz-bypass-governance-retention:true header.
The quotes describe both directions of independence between legal hold and retention period and that any user with s3:PutObjectLegalHold can place or remove a hold.

The quote says lifecycle keeps working on protected objects including delete markers, a locked version cannot be deleted by lifecycle expiration, and Object Lock persists across storage classes and transitions.
The best-practice quotes recommend governance mode when some privileged users need flexibility and compliance mode when no user including root may delete during the retention period.
The quote says Object Lock does not protect against losing or deleting encryption keys and that objects encrypted with SSE-KMS may become unreadable if the KMS key is deleted.
The quote says replication copies locked objects and their retention metadata and that if the source bucket has Object Lock enabled the destination buckets must too.
